item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] War on Iran: How the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps underpins the republic
item.description:
War on Iran: How the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps underpins the republic

Submitted by Daniel Tester on Thu, 09/17/2026 - 13:07
The IRGC has been core to Tehran's influence at home and abroad, not least through Quds Force
Members of the IRGC stand in formation during a "Sacred Defence Week" parade in Tehran in September 2019 (AFP/Iranian presidency handout)
On

 Often called a state within a state, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is a deeply conservative organisation that has underpinned Iran’s establishment for decades and directed much of its response to attacks by the US and Israel this year.

Conceived as a protector of the Iranian revolution, the guard has hundreds of thousands of troops who are distinct from Iran’s official army.

It is also unelected, sitting alongside Iran’s elected officials under the ultimate authority of the supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei. 

The IRGC was founded in March 1979 by commanders of the conservative militias that helped overthrow the western-backed Shah Reza Pahlavi the previous month.

Known as the Pasdaran (“guardians”) or Sepah (“legion”) in Persian, it was established to protect the new political order and to counterbalance Iran’s army, which retained links to the deposed monarchy and, many feared, might stage a coup d’etat.

The IRGC sidelined the leftist factions that helped overthrow the shah, which it opposed ideologically and saw as close to the USSR. 

Today, the guard has five main arms: a ground army, an air force, a navy, an elite overseas wing called Quds Force (meaning “Jerusalem force”) and a volunteer paramilitary called Basij (meaning “mobilisation”).

It is estimated to have 150,000-plus active personnel, plus Basij volunteers who serve as part-time reserves, and whose numbers range from anywhere between 100,000 and 1m. For comparison, Iran’s official army, known domestically as Artesh, has around 600,000 troops.

The IRGC also controls Iran’s ballistic missiles, which it has used to attack Israel, and is tasked with safeguarding border security and the country’s nuclear facilities.

What is the IRGC’s domestic role?

Besides its military role, the guard is embedded in all aspects of life in Iran, from business and politics to education and even sport.

Many IRGC veterans hold senior roles in government and parliament, and can determine the success or failure of an individual's job application or business venture. 

Through Basij, the corps has plainclothes volunteers in neighbourhoods, schools and universities who serve to uphold conservative religious values. Critics have termed the force a “morality police”.

Basij volunteers have also clamped down on political opposition figures and crushed public demonstrations, such as the 1999 student protests, the 2009 Green Movement, and the 2024-2025 protests, when thousands of civilians were killed.

But the IRGC also provides social services (such as after natural disasters) and employment for hundreds of thousands in rural areas, gaining it supporters among parts of the population. 

As an economic force, the IRGC holds hundreds of government contracts, many of which were awarded under the conservative president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad (2005-13).

Through these, it has developed monopolies over industries and now receives an estimated 50 percent of revenues from Iran’s oil sector. 

Thomas Juneau, professor at the University of Ottawa’s Graduate School of Public and International Affairs, told Middle East Eye that the corps’ business interests “allow the IRGC and its sympathisers to themselves profit, to have access to pots of cash with which they can buy off the loyalty of others, and to marginalise competing business interests.

“In that sense, the IRGC has both a vested interest in the survival of the Islamic Republic and its web of cronyism, as well as the means to protect its survival.”

What does the IRGC do outside Iran?

Through Quds Force, the IRGC has long helped fund and supply a network of regional groups that Tehran has dubbed its “Axis of Resistance”. 

These include Hamas in occupied Palestine, Hezbollah in Lebanon, parts of the Hashd al-Shaabi (Popular Mobilisation) umbrella group in Iraq, and Ansar Allah in Yemen, better known as the Houthis. 

Support for Palestine has long been core to the IRGC, and each of these groups has sought to counter Israeli, US and Saudi influence in the region. 

Hamas has fought several wars with Israel and launched the 7 October attacks in 2023; Hezbollah has battled Israel since the 1980s; and the Houthis have hit Israel with drone attacks and blocked shipping lanes in the Red Sea.

Nonetheless, each group retains some independence from Tehran, which for instance denied involvement in Hamas’s 7 October attack - a claim US intelligence has supported. 

The IRGC also supported Bashar al-Assad in Syria prior to and during the civil war, during which hundreds of thousands of people were killed and millions more forced from their homes.

Syria under Assad also long served as a supply channel for Iranian weapons for Hezbollah in Lebanon until his fall in December 2024. 

How did the IRGC become so powerful?

One of the guard's first major roles after the 1979 revolution was suppressing armed rebellions by Kurdish and other minority ethnic groups.

From 1980 until 1988, tens of thousands were killed during the Iran-Iraq War amid battles, minefields and chemical weapons.

Sina Azodi, assistant professor of Middle East politics at George Washington University’s Elliott School of International Affairs, told Middle East Eye that the conflict was pivotal in the guard's development. 

“The current Iranian political leadership were the volunteers of the Iran-Iraq war who with very basic training went to the front lines with nothing more than assault rifles.”

The IRGC's current worldview, he says, was shaped by its memory of the international support for Saddam Hussein's Iraq that it confronted during the conflict.

"Their mindset is shaped by those traumas and the need for Iran to be able to stand on its own feet to defend the country."

The IRGC was tasked with reconstruction after the war, seeing its role grow under new supreme leader Ali Khamenei and expanding an intelligence arm that now rivals the Ministry of Intelligence.

Much of the IRGC’s international network was laid by Qassem Soleimani, Quds Force leader from 1998 until his assassination by the US in 2020 and regarded as the second most powerful person in Iran after Khamenei. 

His killing shocked the IRGC. Five days later, it shot down a Ukrainian commercial passenger plane as it left Tehran’s main airport, killing 176 people onboard. It later apologised, saying that it mistook the aircraft for a military plane.

What action has been taken against the group?

The IRGC is regarded as an adversary by many regional Arab-majority governments and much of the West, where it has long been sanctioned. 

Many governments have gone further, designating the IRGC as a terrorist group, which typically makes it a criminal offence to communicate with, trade with or express support for it or its affiliates.

The US was the first to proscribe the Quds Force in 2007, and banned the IRGC altogether in 2019 during the first administration of President Donald Trump. 

Some officials in the Pentagon and the CIA privately opposed the Trump move: it is diplomatically unusual to ban official parts of other governments. The US considered delisting the IRGC during the Biden administration. 

But other countries soon followed suit. Canada proscribed the IRGC in 2024, as did the EU in January 2026 after the mass killing of Iranian protesters. 

The EU move, led by Italy and supported by France and Spain, has been followed by European countries outside the bloc. The UK proscribed the guard in July amid pressure from the US, years of lobbying from pro-Israel and Iranian diaspora groups, and attacks on Jewish groups in London that the UK government has linked to the IRGC. 

In total, 23 countries, aside from the 27 EU members, have designated the IRGC as a terrorist organisation, including Argentina, Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Israel, Saudi Arabia and Ukraine.

While more than a hundred others have not sanctioned the IRGC, ties with the rest of the world are restricted by secondary sanctions imposed by the US, which sanction any firm that trades with any IRGC affiliates.

The measures have led Iran and the IRGC to strengthen relations with US rivals that have similarly been cut off from the US-dominated financial system, or have enough economic heft to weather potential US retaliation.

The IRGC has sold weapons to Russia throughout its invasion of Ukraine and jet fuel to Myanmar’s junta during the country’s civil war. Iran sells much of its crude oil to China via a so-called “shadow fleet” that aims to skirt US sanctions. 

Who are the IRGC's key figures?

Many of the IRGC’s top personnel have been assassinated by the US and Israel in recent years. Key to its survival has been its succession strategy, with Juneau saying it "has long had extensive contingency plans to replace killed commanders".

Its highest rank is commander-in-chief, one of several IRGC roles directly appointed by the supreme leader. Ahmad Vahidi, previously Iran’s minister of defence, has held that position since his predecessor, Mohammed Pakpour, was killed by Israel in March. He in turn succeeded Hossein Salami whom Israel killed in the June 2025 war. 

Esmail Qaani has led Quds Force since Soleimani’s 2020 assassination. Hossein Taeb, a cleric and former intelligence chief, is current head of Basij after Israel killed Gholamreza Soleimani (no relation to Qassem) in March. 

Others killed by Israel include Alireza Tangsiri, commander of the IRGC Navy, on 26 March, and Majid Khademi, head of the IRGC’s intelligence wing, on 6 April. 

Israeli airstrikes have also targeted more moderate figures, including Ali Larijani, a pragmatic politician who headed Iran’s security council until he was assassinated by Israel on 17 March. It is now led by Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, a longtime IRGC hardliner. 

How has the IRGC been hurt by the war?

Juneau says that “on the one hand, the IRGC has been badly hit by the US and Israel during the war, as have other pillars of the Islamic Republic”. 

“If we simply count strikes, military installations damaged or destroyed, ships or aircraft damaged or destroyed, then we can conclude that the IRGC has been significantly weakened,” he says. 

But the guard “has prepared for this war for decades”, he adds.

“The US and Israel have destroyed an important proportion of the IRGC's missiles and drones, but the force still has more than enough to continue threatening shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.”  

For this reason, Juneau says the IRGC is far from admitting defeat, with many hardliners believing they have the upper hand and seeing no need to make compromises. 

“The way out of the war to the IRGC is to consolidate and institutionalise its geopolitical gains.

“It wants, in particular, to see a new arrangement in the Persian Gulf whereby it can de facto veto maritime traffic.”

How the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps underpins Iran

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Qatar pushes for revival of US-Iran talks, warns against ‘cycles of escalation’
item.description:
Qatar pushes for revival of US-Iran talks, warns against ‘cycles of escalation’

Qatar is working to restart negotiations between the United States and Iran, its foreign ministry said on Sunday, as the prime minister warned that regional security cannot rest on repeated confrontation.

A ministry spokesperson said Qatari officials were “shuttling between capitals” in the hope of making progress, and that Doha had received assurances from US administration officials that Washington wants to reach an agreement.

The spokesperson called for a regional solution that delivers stability, alongside an international understanding that protects waterways such as the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking also on Sunday, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani said lasting security could not be built through "repeated cycles of escalation and retaliation", nor through "arrangements that leave any state vulnerable to the absence of security".

He called for a framework in which sovereignty is respected, and no state can pose a "threat to another", adding that Qatar “had worked with regional and international partners to keep channels of communication open and reduce tensions.”

In a statement, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry has condemned the storming of the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound by Ben Gvir and Israeli settlers on Sunday, saying “repeated provocations will fuel cycles of violence and escalation in the region”.

The Houthis have declared what they call an "equation of blockade for blockade and escalation for escalation", vowing that Riyadh will face consequences for restrictions imposed on Yemen.

Mahdi al-Mashat, who heads the group's Supreme Political Council, said in a televised address that Yemen was pressing ahead to end the Saudi campaign and the blockade, reopen its airports and seaports, recover national resources, and secure compensation.

He said shipping and international commerce passing through the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab faced no threat from Yemen, with Saudi vessels the sole exception.

Separately, Houthi political bureau member Mohamed al-Bukhaiti said in an interview with the Associated Press on Sunday that the group had given the Trump administration assurances it would not strike American ships in the Red Sea.

He said Washington had contacted Houthis following their swift push along Yemen's western coastline towards the Bab al-Mandab Strait earlier this month.

Only Saudi Arabia was being targeted in the waterway, al-Bukhaiti affirmed.

item.description:
‘I'm so, so sorry’: Ed Sheeran addresses Gaza on stage after losing every opening act

About a week after the widespread international backlash for dropping his pro-Palestinian support act, Ed Sheeran made his first public comments on stage, apologising to fans and saying that what Israel is doing in Gaza is "unjustifiable".

Last week, American rapper Macklemore announced online that he had been removed from Sheeran's Loop Tour, which is due to stop at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, where Sheeran has shows on 25 and 26 September.

Macklemore was to open for Sheeran, but the stadium's owner, Robert Kraft, wanted him removed over his pro-Palestine speeches on stage, threatening to cancel Sheeran's stadium concerts if he stayed, and lobbying other stadium owners to join him in applying pressure.

"I've had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I'm so, so sorry," Sheeran told his audience in Philadelphia, where he performed for the first time since Macklemore was taken off the tour.

Pro-Palestinian protesters gathered outside the venue hours before Sheeran's concert was due to start.

At the start of the concert at Lincoln Financial Field, Sheeran called Israel's war on Gaza "catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate".

According to US media reports, the start time of Sheeran's concert was pushed back by two and a half hours because of the withdrawal of all the opening acts, and Sheeran performed solo.

Read more: ‘I'm so, so sorry’: Ed Sheeran addresses Gaza on stage after losing every opening act

item.description:
Gaza authorities announce plan to demolish 255 war-damaged buildings

Gaza’s Government Media Office has announced the launching an "urgent emergency plan", where 255 buildings damaged by Israeli attacks across the besieged enclave will be demolished.

"As part of the comprehensive management of this crisis, relevant ministries have issued strict directives to their departments to immediately initiate field operations and implement the evacuation plan," the office said in a press release on Sunday.

"These directives include issuing formal notices to the owners of hazardous buildings requiring immediate evacuation, installing warning signs to prevent access, and arranging temporary shelter for affected families."

However, the office outlined a number of challenges, including some families refusing to evacuate, lack of funding, shortages of equipment and machinery due to Israel's ongoing siege as well as a lack of land to shelter evacuated families. 

The announcement follows the collapse of a building damaged by Israeli bombardment last week in Gaza City.

The six-storey building, which had four apartments per floor and was housing at least 100 displaced people, crumbled overnight onto nearby homes and tents in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City. 

At least 21 displaced Palestinians, including five children, were killed as a result.

Intergenerational report predicts that in four decades’ time, more Australians will be dying than being born each year

Labor says better investment in early childhood education and care, such as a possible move to universal access for families, is a better way to address Australia’s declining birthrate, rejecting the need for a new “baby bonus”.

Monday’s intergenerational report showed that more Australians will be dying than being born in 40 years’ time, a milestone already experienced by countries including South Korea, Italy, Germany and Japan.
